'''''Euphorbia paralias''''', the '''sea spurge''',<ref>{{cite book |author1=David Chapman |title=Exploring the Cornish Coast |date=2008 |publisher=Alison Hodge |location=[[Penzance]] |isbn=9780906720561 |page=45}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Euphorbiaceae]], native to [[Europe]], northern [[Africa]] and western [[Asia]].<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=2008-12-23}}</ref>

The species is widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in [[Australia]].<ref name=NSW/> It invades coastal areas, displacing local species and colonising open sand areas favoured by certain nesting birds.<ref name=weed>{{cite web |title=Have you seen this beach weed? |publisher=Department of Primary Industries, Water and Environment (Tasmania) |url=http://www.environment.tas.gov.au/file.aspx?id=2204 |access-date=30 May 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110422150118/http://www.environment.tas.gov.au/file.aspx?id=2204 |archive-date=22 April 2011}}</ref> Major eradication programs have been undertaken in some areas, for example by [[Sea Spurge Remote Area Teams]] in [[Tasmania]], with great success.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wildcare SPRATS volunteer weed eradication project |url=http://www.parks.tas.gov.au/file.aspx?base=41336 |publisher=Parks and Wildlife Service Tasmania |access-date=2023-11-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171207140655if_/http://www.parks.tas.gov.au/file.aspx?base=41336 |archive-date=2017-12-07}}</ref> A small colony of over 50 plants was discovered at a location on Ninety Mile Beach, Northland in New Zealand in July 2025 where it has believed to have came from sea currents coming from Australia.<ref>https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/567227/toxic-highly-invasive-pest-plant-found-at-far-north-beach</ref> 7 other locations in Northland have also had colonies or plants found in the past 12 months prior to the discovery in July though the species has been recorded being present since 2012.

==Description==
''Euphorbia paralias'' is an erect, glaucous, [[perennial plant]], growing up to {{convert|70|cm|in}} tall. It has many stems, dividing into 3–5 fertile branches, each branching further. The cauline leaves (arising from the stem, without a stalk) are crowded, overlapping, elliptic-ovate (ovate toward the top of the stems), fleshy and {{convert|5|-|20|mm|1}} long. Leaves on fertile branches are circular-rhombic or [[reniform leaf|reniform]]. The flower head is on a solitary [[cyathium]], found in upper forks or at the apex, surrounded by bell-shaped [[Bract|bracts]]. Female flowers have [[Style (botany)|styles]] that divide into two short [[Stigma (botany)|stigmas]], flowering from September to May. The fruit is a capsule, flattened from above or nearly spherical, with deep furrows, and wrinkled on keels. Seeds are ovoid, pale-grey and smooth. There is a kidney-shaped fleshy outgrowth from the seed coat.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Boyce |first1=Lauran |last2=Buckeridge |first2=John |title=The terrestrial plants of the Rickett's Point Urban Sanctuary : Beaumaris Vic 3193 |date=2018 |publisher=Greypath Productions |location=Beaumaris, Victoria |isbn=978-1760019716 |page=73 |url= https://mesac.org.au/newsletters-mesac/|access-date=7 November 2020}}</ref><ref name=NSW>{{cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Euphorbia~paralias |title=''Euphorbia paralias'' |access-date=2008-12-23 |author=  James, T.A. & G.J. Harden
|work= PlantNET – New South Wales Flora Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust, Sydney Australia}}</ref>

==Habitat==
This species inhabits sandy sea-shores.<ref name="FEU">{{cite book |title=Flora Europaea, vol. 2 |author=Tutin}}</ref>
